reviews.reasoning: The rule parses and the fields Image, DestinationIp and DestinationPort are valid. The values '198.51.100.', 8080, 8000, chrome.exe and msedge.exe all occur in the two verbatim quotes. DestinationIp|startswith '198.51.100.' is the right way to express the /24, since cidr is not allowed. It is also an 11-character positive term on a non-process field, which satisfies the breadth guard. The 3 positives match, including the unobserved host .131 and the non-browser binaries. The chrome and msedge look-alikes are removed by filter_browser. The powershell look-alike at 192.0.2.50:8080 is outside the prefix. The negatives are on ports 443 and 80, so they do not match. T1571 is the only tag pair and is correct.
incidental_issues: filter_browser excludes chrome.exe and msedge.exe on port 8000 as well, although the report exempts browsers only on 8080 (minor over-exclusion).
The browser exclusion is by image name only, so an attacker binary named chrome.exe would evade the rule.
Ports 8080 and 8000 are common alternate web ports, so T1571 is a modest stretch, though the case cites it.

reviews.reasoning: The single regex '^[0-9a-f]{20,}\.relay-hub\.example$' on QueryName uses the allowed 're' modifier, and pySigma parses it. Its literal runs ('relay-hub', 'example') occur in the verbatim quote 'under the zone relay-hub.example'. I checked the hex labels by hand: the positives 9f2a61c0d4e87b35a1c2e7 (22 chars) and c04d7e91b2a85f36d9e0143a (24 chars) are all within [0-9a-f] and at least 20 long, so both match. The look-alikes status. (non-hex) and a1b2c3d4e5f6 (12 chars) fail the pattern, and the negatives are unrelated domains. incidental_issues: The rule does not constrain Image, which is fine given the report, but the hex test relies on case-insensitive matching, so uppercase hex would also match.
Whether Wazuh's regex engine accepts the {20,} quantifier cannot be verified from the contract, which lists 're' as allowed.
